meta.title: Banking Regulation – 2023
meta.description: 370 MCQs covering Nigerian banking regulation, supervision, and CAMELS

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes banking regulation in Nigeria?
opts: Laws enacted by the National Assembly and subsidiary legislations by the CBN and NDIC.
Only the CBN Act and BOFIA, with no subsidiary rules.
Guidelines issued exclusively by the Federal Ministry of Finance.
International treaties that automatically apply without local enactment.
questionBank.exp: Banking regulation comprises laws by the National Assembly and subsidiary legislations (regulations, guidelines, directives) by the CBN and NDIC (Trainee Manual, p.2).

questionBank.q: The period from 1894 to 1952 in Nigerian banking history is described as:
questionBank.exp: 1894–1952 is referred to as the era of free banking due to total absence of regulation (Trainee Manual, p.2).

questionBank.q: What major regulatory development occurred in 1952 regarding Nigerian banks?
opts: The Central Bank of Nigeria was established.
The Banking Ordinance introduced licensing and minimum paid-up capital.
The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Act compelled indigenisation.
The Banking Act of 1968 was first enacted.
questionBank.exp: The Banking Ordinance of 1952 introduced licensing and minimum paid-up capital requirements, marking the start of regulation (p.2).

questionBank.q: The Central Bank of Nigeria Act was enacted in 1958, but it commenced operations in:
questionBank.exp: The CBN Act was passed in 1958 but operations began in 1959 (p.2).

questionBank.q: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Act (Decree) of 1972 compelled:
opts: The participation of Nigerians and the Federal Government in foreign banks' equities.
The consolidation of all banks into one national bank.
The establishment of the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation.
The adoption of the Basel Accord.
questionBank.exp: The 1972 Act compelled participation of Nigerians and the Federal Government in acquiring controlling equities of foreign banks (p.2).

questionBank.q: What was the main outcome of the liberalisation era (1984–1992)?
opts: Reduction in the number of banks from 89 to 25.
The number of licensed banks rose from 24 to 120 by 1992.
The establishment of the Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee.
The introduction of the Prudential Guidelines.
questionBank.exp: Liberalisation removed stringent rules, and by end of 1992, licensed banks increased to 120 (p.3).

questionBank.q: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) was established in:
questionBank.exp: NDIC was established in 1988 to insure deposit liabilities and handle bank failures; commenced operations in 1989 (p.3).

questionBank.q: The Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) was first enacted in:
questionBank.exp: BOFIA was enacted in 1991 to strengthen regulatory and supervisory structures (p.3).

questionBank.q: The Banking Consolidation program initiated in 2004 raised the minimum capitalisation of banks from ₦4 billion to:
questionBank.exp: The consolidation program raised minimum capital from ₦4bn to ₦25bn; by Dec 2006, 25 banks emerged from 89 (p.3).

questionBank.q: Which regulatory agency has the primary objective of ensuring monetary and price stability in Nigeria?
questionBank.exp: CBN's principal objectives include ensuring monetary and price stability (p.4).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Central Bank of Nigeria as stated in the CBN Act?
opts: Acting as banker to the Federal Government.
questionBank.exp: Deposit insurance is a function of NDIC, not CBN. CBN issues currency, maintains reserves, advises the government, and acts as banker to other banks (p.4).

questionBank.q: The Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) complements the CBN by:
opts: Conducting on-site supervision of banks exclusively.
Insuring customers' deposits and handling bank failure resolutions.
Setting monetary policy and interest rates.
questionBank.exp: NDIC insures deposits and shares supervision with CBN; it also handles liquidation of failed banks (p.5).

questionBank.q: Under Section 2 of the NDIC Act 2006, which of the following is a function of the NDIC?
opts: Structuring liquidation of insured institutions as a last resort.
questionBank.exp: NDIC functions include insuring deposits, assisting monetary authorities, supervising banks, and structuring liquidation when licences are revoked (p.5).

questionBank.q: The Federal Ministry of Finance (FMF) primarily handles:
opts: Fiscal policy, tax revenue, and supervision of NDIC, SEC, NAICOM, etc.
questionBank.exp: FMF is in charge of fiscal policy and oversees NDIC, SEC, NAICOM, Customs, FIRS, etc. (p.5).

questionBank.q: Which regulatory authority is the apex body for the Nigerian capital market?
questionBank.exp: SEC is the apex regulatory authority for the capital market, registering securities, exchanges, issuing houses, and stockbroking firms (p.5).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a function of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)?
questionBank.exp: SEC approves and regulates mergers and acquisitions, authorises unit trusts, and monitors the capital market (p.5-6).

questionBank.q: The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) is empowered to investigate all financial crimes, including:
questionBank.exp: Section 6 of EFCC Act lists advance fee fraud, money laundering, counterfeiting, computer credit card fraud, contract scam, etc. (p.6).

questionBank.q: The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) was established in 1995 mainly to:
opts: Combat money laundering arising from drug trafficking.
Issue banking licences to financial institutions.
questionBank.exp: NDLEA's main objective is to interdict, investigate, and prosecute money laundering from illicit drug dealings (p.6).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a member of the Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee (FSRCC)?
questionBank.exp: FSRCC members: CBN (Chairman), SEC, NAICOM, CAC, FMF, NDIC, PENCOM. EFCC is not a member (p.7).

questionBank.q: The main objective of the Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee (FSRCC) is to:
opts: Coordinate supervision and reduce arbitrage among regulatory authorities.
Issue banking licences to new banks.
Set interest rates for bank loans.
questionBank.exp: FSRCC aims for coordinated supervision, reducing arbitrage, sharing information, and promoting sound practices (p.7).

questionBank.q: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision was established in 1974 after the failure of:
opts: Bank of Credit and Commerce International.
questionBank.exp: The Herstatt Bank liquidation on June 26, 1974, due to time-zone settlement failure, prompted the establishment of the Basel Committee (p.8).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is true about the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision?
opts: It has supranational supervisory authority over all member countries.
Its conclusions have legal force in all G10 countries.
It provides a forum for cooperation and does not possess formal legal authority.
It was established by the United Nations.
questionBank.exp: The Committee does not possess formal supranational authority; its conclusions were never intended to have legal force (p.8).

questionBank.q: The Basel Accord of 1988 (Basel I) primarily focused on:
questionBank.exp: Basel I focused on capital adequacy and minimum capital requirements (p.8).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a pillar of Basel II?
questionBank.exp: Basel II has three pillars: minimum capital requirements, supervisory review, and market discipline (p.8-9).

questionBank.q: Under Pillar III of Basel II, banks are required to:
opts: Disclose financial and other information to allow market participants to assess capital adequacy.
Maintain a minimum liquidity coverage ratio.
Submit to on-site examinations twice a year.
Obtain approval for all new products.
questionBank.exp: Pillar III aims to complement capital requirements and supervisory review with disclosure requirements for market discipline (p.9).

questionBank.q: Basel III placed a new emphasis on:
opts: Market risk and interest rate risk.
questionBank.exp: Basel III, after the 2007-2009 crisis, emphasised liquidity standards to prevent lack of ready cash (p.9).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a 'Core Principle for Effective Banking Supervision' issued by the Basel Committee?
opts: All banks must have a minimum of 25% capital adequacy.
Supervisors must have the power to revoke licences and take corrective actions.
Banks are prohibited from lending to directors.
All banks must be owned by the government.
questionBank.exp: The Core Principles include supervisory powers such as licence revocation and corrective actions. The others are not principles (p.10).

questionBank.q: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank were created in 1944 at:
questionBank.exp: Both institutions were established at the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944 (p.10).

questionBank.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the IMF from the World Bank?
opts: The IMF focuses on long-term development, while the World Bank focuses on macroeconomic stability.
The IMF focuses on macroeconomic issues, while the World Bank concentrates on long-term economic development and poverty reduction.
The IMF provides loans, while the World Bank only offers grants.
The IMF is a UN agency, but the World Bank is independent.
questionBank.exp: IMF focuses on macroeconomics, World Bank on development and poverty reduction (p.10).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why banks are heavily regulated?
opts: To safeguard individual deposits and sustain public trust.
To maximise bank profitability and shareholder returns.
To prevent money laundering and other financial crimes.
questionBank.exp: Regulation is not designed to maximise profits; it aims to protect depositors, ensure stability, and combat crime (p.3).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a direct regulator of banks in Nigeria?
questionBank.exp: CBN is a direct regulator; FMF, SEC, EFCC are indirect regulators (p.4-6).

questionBank.q: The CBN has exclusive supervisory authority over which of the following financial institutions?
opts: Deposit money banks (in collaboration with NDIC).
Finance companies and Bureau de Change.
questionBank.exp: CBN exclusively supervises finance companies, Bureaux de change, mortgage institutions, and discount houses (p.4).

questionBank.q: The NDIC's deposit insurance covers:
opts: All deposit liabilities of licensed banks and such other financial institutions.
Only deposits of commercial banks up to ₦500,000.
Only savings accounts, not current accounts.
questionBank.exp: Section 2 of NDIC Act states it insures all deposit liabilities of licensed banks and other financial institutions (p.5).

questionBank.q: Which indirect regulator is responsible for registering and regulating stock exchanges?
questionBank.exp: SEC registers and regulates stock exchanges, over-the-counter transactions, and other investment exchanges (p.5).

questionBank.q: The EFCC was established to coordinate and enforce all economic and financial crimes laws. This is stated in:
questionBank.exp: Section 6 of the EFCC Act confers these powers (p.6).

questionBank.q: Which agency has the power to place bank accounts under surveillance and tap telephone lines in the course of investigating drug-related money laundering?
questionBank.exp: NDLEA is empowered to place accounts under surveillance, tap telephones, access computer systems, etc. (p.6).

questionBank.q: The Financial Services Regulation Coordinating Committee (FSRCC) includes which of the following?
opts: Nigerian Stock Exchange as a permanent member.
questionBank.exp: FSRCC members: CBN, SEC, NAICOM, CAC, FMF, NDIC, PENCOM. NSE has observer status (p.7).

questionBank.q: One of the objectives of the FSRCC is to:
opts: Eliminate information gaps encountered by regulatory agencies.
Set interest rates for all banks.
questionBank.exp: Objectives include coordinated supervision, reducing arbitrage, deliberating on problems, eliminating information gaps, and promoting sound practices (p.7).

questionBank.q: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision was originally established by the G10 countries along with:
questionBank.exp: The Committee was formed by G10 countries plus Switzerland and Luxembourg under the auspices of the BIS (p.8).

questionBank.q: Pillar II of Basel II provides:
questionBank.exp: Pillar II is about supervisory review and gives regulators tools to deal with systemic, pension, concentration, strategic, reputational, liquidity, and legal risks (p.8).

questionBank.q: The Basel III Accord was introduced in response to:
opts: The European sovereign debt crisis of 2010.
questionBank.exp: Basel III was issued in December 2010 in response to the 2007-2009 crisis (p.9).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the supervisory structure for banking regulation as identified by the Basel Core Principles?
questionBank.exp: The four components are: legal/institutional structure, regulatory structure, supervisory structure, and safety net arrangements (p.10).

questionBank.q: The CBN's function of acting as banker to other banks is intended to:
opts: Ensure commercial banks maintain high profits.
Seek cooperation of banks in performing its functions under the Act.
questionBank.exp: CBN acts as banker to banks and seeks their cooperation in performing its functions (p.4).

questionBank.q: The Nigerian banking regulatory environment includes both direct and indirect regulators. Which of the following is an indirect regulator?
opts: Both NDIC and CBN are direct.
questionBank.exp: Direct regulators are CBN and NDIC; indirect include FMF, SEC, EFCC, NDLEA, etc. (p.4-6).

questionBank.q: The Banking Act of 1968 is significant because:
opts: It introduced the first comprehensive regulatory and supervisory framework.
questionBank.exp: The Banking Act of 1968 codified rules and presented the first comprehensive attempt at institutionalising a standard framework (p.2).

questionBank.q: The era of indigenisation (1972-1976) under the Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Decree led to:
opts: Nigerian participation in foreign banks' ownership.
questionBank.exp: The Decree compelled participation of Nigerians and the Federal Government in acquiring controlling equities of foreign banks (p.2-3).

questionBank.q: In the liberalisation era (1984-1992), the CBN established the deposit protection scheme in 1988 to:
opts: Encourage foreign banks to enter Nigeria.
Handle the consequences of bank failures.
questionBank.exp: The deposit protection scheme was established to handle consequences of bank failures (p.3).

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the universal banking structure that was revoked by the CBN in 2009?
opts: Banks could only engage in commercial banking activities.
Banks were allowed to engage in a wide range of financial services under one licence.
Banks were required to form holding companies.
Banks were prohibited from investing in non-bank subsidiaries.
questionBank.exp: The CBN revoked universal banking and introduced the holding company structure (p.3).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to request and share information on matters affecting the economy is part of its:
questionBank.exp: CBN is empowered to request and share information as part of its supervision and regulation (p.4).

questionBank.q: Which agency is responsible for approving and regulating unit trusts (mutual funds)?
questionBank.exp: SEC authorises the establishment of unit trusts (p.6).

questionBank.q: The NDIC's function of 'guaranteeing payments to depositors' is capped at a maximum amount as provided in:
questionBank.exp: Section 20 of NDIC Act provides for maximum deposit insurance coverage (p.5).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a function of the CBN that requires the approval of the President?
opts: Acting as banker to the Federal Government.
questionBank.exp: CBN has sole right of issuing currency but requires Presidential approval to redenominate (p.4).

questionBank.q: The 'era of free banking' in Nigeria ended with the enactment of:
opts: The Nigerian Enterprises Promotion Act of 1972.
questionBank.exp: Banking regulation started with the 1952 Banking Ordinance, ending the free banking era (p.2).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a 'safety net arrangement' as described in the Basel Core Principles?
opts: Deposit insurance scheme or winding-up procedures.
questionBank.exp: Safety net arrangements handle liquidity and solvency difficulties and include deposit insurance or winding-up procedures (p.10).

questionBank.q: The CBN's supervisory role is exercised in collaboration with the NDIC for deposit money banks, but the CBN exclusively supervises:
opts: Finance companies and Bureaux de change.
questionBank.exp: CBN exclusively supervises finance companies, Bureaux de change, mortgage institutions, and discount houses (p.4).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an objective of the FSRCC?
opts: To reduce arbitrage opportunities created by differing regulatory standards.
To merge all regulatory agencies into one.
questionBank.exp: FSRCC aims to reduce arbitrage opportunities and coordinate supervision (p.7).

questionBank.q: The Basel Committee's origins can be traced to the failure of Bank Herstatt, which highlighted:
opts: Settlement risk due to time-zone differences.
questionBank.exp: Bank Herstatt's failure was due to time-zone differences in payment settlements (p.8).

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the IMF and the World Bank?
opts: Both were created at Bretton Woods and share the same goal of raising living standards.
IMF provides long-term development loans; World Bank stabilises exchange rates.
They are both agencies of the United Nations with identical mandates.
The World Bank is a division of the IMF.
questionBank.exp: Both were created at Bretton Woods in 1944 and share the goal of raising living standards, though their approaches differ (p.10).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a principal objective of the CBN as stated in the CBN Act?
opts: Provide economic and financial advice to the Federal Government.
questionBank.exp: CBN's objectives do not include capital market regulation; that is SEC's role (p.4).

questionBank.q: The NDIC's role in liquidation of failed banks is to ensure:
opts: Assets are sold to the highest bidder, irrespective of depositors.
Orderly and efficient liquidation and cost-effective realisation of assets.
The government takes over all liabilities.
questionBank.exp: NDIC ensures orderly liquidation and cost-effective realisation of assets, with proceeds appropriated among claimants (p.5).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to arrange for the printing of currency notes and minting of coins falls under its:
questionBank.exp: The CBN has sole right of issuing currency, and arranges printing and minting (p.4).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a function of the SEC that directly impacts banks?
opts: Approving mergers and acquisitions involving banks.
Setting capital adequacy ratios for banks.
questionBank.exp: SEC approves and regulates mergers and acquisitions (p.5-6).

questionBank.q: The EFCC's power to freeze, confiscate, or seize proceeds derived from terrorist activities is provided under:
questionBank.exp: Section 6(d) of EFCC Act empowers the commission to adopt measures to identify, trace, freeze, confiscate or seize proceeds of terrorist activities and economic/financial crimes (p.6).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an indirect regulator that has the power to access bank records and private contracts?
questionBank.exp: NDLEA is empowered to obtain communication of authentic instruments and all bank, financial, and commercial records (p.6).

questionBank.q: The Basel Committee's first Accord (Basel I) was motivated by concerns over:
opts: Low capital levels of internationally active banks and competitive advantages.
Excessive liquidity in the banking system.
questionBank.exp: Basel I was motivated by low capital levels and competitive advantages of banks with lower capital requirements (p.8).

questionBank.q: Under Basel II, Pillar III's market discipline is achieved through:
opts: Mandatory disclosure requirements that allow stakeholders to assess risk.
questionBank.exp: Pillar III requires public disclosure to enable investors, analysts, and customers to assess the bank's capital adequacy and risk (p.9).

questionBank.q: The Nigerian banking sector's adoption of the Basel Accords is intended to:
opts: Align Nigeria with international best practices and reduce systemic risk.
questionBank.exp: Adoption of Basel Accords aims to maintain international best practice and establish sustainable risk-management practices (p.4).

questionBank.q: Which of the following regulatory bodies was established primarily to handle the consequences of bank failures?
questionBank.exp: NDIC was established to insure deposits and handle bank failures (p.3).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines of 1990 were introduced to:
opts: Standardise asset classification and loan loss provisioning.
Increase bank capital requirements to ₦25 billion.
questionBank.exp: The Prudential Guidelines were meant to guide asset classification and loan loss provisioning (p.3, p.19).

questionBank.q: The CBN's stress testing and restructuring of banks from 2009 aimed to:
opts: Revoke the universal banking structure and introduce holding company structure.
Reduce the number of banks from 120 to 25.
Increase the minimum capital to ₦4 billion.
questionBank.exp: From 2009, CBN engaged in stress testing, restructuring, revoked universal banking, and introduced holding company structure (p.3).

questionBank.q: Which of the following best defines 'regulation' in the context of banking?
opts: A process of supervising bank employees.
An official rule or order stating what may or may not be done.
A recommendation issued by the IMF.
A voluntary code of conduct for banks.
questionBank.exp: Regulation means an official rule, law, or order stating what may or may not be done (p.10).

questionBank.q: 'Supervision' in banking refers to:
opts: Watching over an activity to ensure it is performed as required.
The process of setting capital ratios.
questionBank.exp: Supervision means to watch over an activity or task and ensure it is performed as required (p.11).

questionBank.q: Why must banks adapt their operational frameworks when regulations change?
opts: To comply with the law and reduce risk.
To increase profits and reduce costs.
To prevent any changes in their business.
questionBank.exp: Banks must adapt to comply with law, reduce risk, improve efficiency, and remain competitive (p.11).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a general principle of banking regulation?
opts: Banks must always maintain a loan-to-deposit ratio of 100%.
Banks require a licence from the CBN before engaging in banking business.
Banks are free to set their own capital requirements.
Banks need not disclose financial information to the public.
questionBank.exp: Licensing is a key principle; banks need a CBN licence (p.12).

questionBank.q: Market discipline in banking regulation is achieved through:
questionBank.exp: Market discipline requires banks to publicly disclose information so that depositors and creditors can assess risk (p.12).

questionBank.q: Prudential requirements imposed on banks are typically tied to:
opts: The level of risk exposure of the bank.
The location of the bank's headquarters.
questionBank.exp: Prudential requirements are closely tied to the level of risk exposure (p.12).

questionBank.q: Failure resolution processes in banking regulation are designed to:
opts: Handle distress and bank failure in the best interest of depositors and the economy.
questionBank.exp: Failure resolution processes handle distress and bank failure in the best interest of depositors and the economy (p.12).

questionBank.q: Under Section 2 of BOFIA 2020, banking business in Nigeria can only be carried out by:
opts: A company duly incorporated in Nigeria with a valid banking licence from CBN.
A foreign bank with a representative office.
Any financial institution registered with SEC.
questionBank.exp: Section 2: Only a company incorporated in Nigeria with a valid CBN licence can engage in banking business (p.13).

questionBank.q: Under Section 6 of BOFIA, a bank cannot open a new branch without:
opts: The prior consent of the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Section 6: No bank may open or close any branch without prior CBN consent (p.13).

questionBank.q: Section 9 of BOFIA empowers the CBN to:
opts: Determine the capital requirement for each category of banks.
questionBank.exp: Section 9: CBN has powers to determine capital requirement for each category of banks (p.13).

questionBank.q: Under Section 12 of BOFIA, which of the following is a ground for revocation of a bank's licence?
opts: Failure to pay dividends for two consecutive years.
Conducting business in an unsound manner.
Opening a branch without board approval.
Having a capital adequacy ratio below 15%.
questionBank.exp: Section 12 lists grounds including conducting business in an unsound manner, insufficient assets, failure to comply with obligations, etc. (p.13-14).

questionBank.q: Section 13 of BOFIA requires all banks to maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio (CAR) as prescribed by CBN. Failure to do so may lead to:
questionBank.exp: Section 13: penalties for failure may include revocation of licence (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 14 of BOFIA requires banks to maintain with the CBN:
opts: A copy of all loan agreements.
questionBank.exp: Section 14: Banks must maintain cash reserves, special deposits, and specified liquid assets with CBN (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 15 and 16 of BOFIA require banks to maintain a reserve fund and may only declare dividends from:
opts: Net profit after provision for tax, expenses, and losses.
questionBank.exp: Sections 15 & 16: Dividend can only be declared from net profit after tax, expenses, and losses (p.14).

questionBank.q: Under Section 17 of BOFIA, directors and officers of a bank must:
opts: Disclose any interest they have in a credit facility.
Receive prior approval from SEC for all loans.
Maintain a fixed deposit with the bank.
Not hold shares in the bank.
questionBank.exp: Section 17: Directors, managers, or officers must disclose any interest in a credit facility and ensure adequate security (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 18 of BOFIA prohibits a bank from having as a director a person who:
opts: Is a director of any other bank, unless approved by CBN.
questionBank.exp: Section 18: No bank shall have a director who is a director of any other bank without CBN approval, and cannot re-employ persons convicted of fraud (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 19(1)(a) of BOFIA restricts a commercial bank from granting loans to a single obligor exceeding:
opts: 20% of the bank's shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses.
questionBank.exp: Section 19(1)(a): For a commercial bank, the single obligor limit is 20% of shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 19(1)(a) provides that for a merchant bank, the single obligor limit is:
questionBank.exp: Section 19(1)(a): Merchant bank single obligor limit is 50% of shareholders' fund (p.14).

questionBank.q: Section 19(3)(a) prohibits unsecured advances to directors and significant shareholders above an aggregate amount of:
questionBank.exp: Section 19(3)(a): Unsecured advances to directors or significant shareholders above ₦1,000,000 or such amount as prescribed is prohibited (p.14-15).

questionBank.q: Under Section 19(3)(b), unsecured advances to officers and employees must not exceed:
questionBank.exp: Section 19(3)(b): Unsecured advances to officers and employees must not exceed one year's emolument (p.15).

questionBank.q: Section 33 of BOFIA empowers the Governor of CBN to order a special examination of a bank if:
opts: The bank applies for a licence.
It is in the public interest to do so.
The bank opens a new branch.
questionBank.exp: Section 33: CBN Governor may order special examination if public interest, detrimental conduct, insufficient assets, contravention, or application by director/shareholder (p.15).

questionBank.q: Section 34 of BOFIA grants the CBN intervention powers if a bank is likely to become unable to meet its obligations. This is triggered when:
opts: The bank informs the CBN of such situation.
The bank fails to declare dividends.
The bank opens a branch abroad.
questionBank.exp: Section 34: If a bank informs CBN that it is likely to become unable to meet obligations, the Governor may exercise intervention powers (p.15).

questionBank.q: Section 36 of BOFIA defines a systemic banking crisis when, among other conditions, critically distressed banks control:
opts: 10% or more of total industry assets.
12.5% or more of total industry assets.
15% or more of total industry assets.
20% or more of total industry assets.
questionBank.exp: Section 36: Systemic crisis exists when critically distressed banks control 12.5% or more of total industry assets (p.15).

questionBank.q: Section 41 of BOFIA allows the CBN to transfer assets of a failing bank to a private asset management vehicle, such as:
questionBank.exp: Section 41: CBN may transfer assets to one or more private asset management vehicles, e.g., AMCON (p.16).

questionBank.q: Section 44 of BOFIA prohibits:
opts: Persons other than banks from inviting deposits through advertising.
Banks from paying interest on savings.
questionBank.exp: Section 44: Only banks and authorised persons may invite deposits via advertisements (p.16).

questionBank.q: Section 46 of BOFIA prohibits directors and employees of banks from receiving commissions or gifts for rendering banking services. This is to:
questionBank.exp: Section 46 prohibits receipt of commissions, gifts, or property for rendering banking services, to prevent bribery (p.16).

questionBank.q: Under Section 47(1) of BOFIA, before appointing a director or chief executive, a bank must:
opts: Publish a notice in the newspaper.
questionBank.exp: Section 47(1): Banks must seek and obtain CBN's written approval for appointments of directors, CEOs, and specified management staff (p.16).

questionBank.q: Section 47(2) disqualifies a person from being a director or officer if that person:
opts: Has been a director of another bank.
questionBank.exp: Section 47(2): Disqualifications include unsound mind, dismissed from government service, declared bankrupt, convicted of fraud, etc. (p.16).

questionBank.q: Section 49 of BOFIA prescribes penalties for directors and managers who fail to ensure compliance with the Act. The penalty is:
opts: Imprisonment for a term not less than three years or fine of not less than ₦2,000,000.
questionBank.exp: Section 49: Offence is punishable with fine of not less than ₦2,000,000 or imprisonment for not less than three years, or both (p.16-17).

questionBank.q: Section 50 of BOFIA provides for penalties for offences not otherwise provided for, which is a fine of not less than:
questionBank.exp: Section 50: Fine of not less than ₦2,000,000 for contraventions not expressly provided for (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 51 of BOFIA provides protection against adverse claims for the CBN and its officers, provided they acted:
questionBank.exp: Section 51: CBN and officers are protected if they acted in good faith (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 52 of BOFIA confers exclusive jurisdiction to try offences under the Act on:
questionBank.exp: Section 52: Federal High Court has exclusive jurisdiction (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 53 of BOFIA states that the provisions of the Act shall prevail over other laws. This is known as the:
questionBank.exp: Section 53: Supremacy of BOFIA, it prevails over other laws in so far as they relate to banks (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 55 of BOFIA provides that in the liquidation of a bank, deposit liabilities shall have:
questionBank.exp: Section 55: Deposit liabilities shall have priority over all other liabilities (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 56 of BOFIA empowers the Governor of CBN to make rules and regulations for:
opts: The operation and control of all institutions under CBN supervision.
questionBank.exp: Section 56: Governor may make rules and regulations for all institutions under CBN supervision (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 64 of BOFIA allows the CBN to carry out examination of:
opts: The bank and entities associated with or affiliated to it.
questionBank.exp: Section 64: CBN may examine books of banks and entities associated with or affiliated to them (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 67 of BOFIA empowers the Governor to make regulations on corporate governance, including:
questionBank.exp: Section 67: Regulations may cover corporate governance, appointment of principal officers, prohibition on mutual holding of shares, and risk management (p.17).

questionBank.q: Section 70 of BOFIA allows the Governor to designate a bank as:
questionBank.exp: Section 70: Governor may designate a bank as systemically important (p.17-18).

questionBank.q: Section 71 of BOFIA gives CBN power to regulate:
questionBank.exp: Section 71: CBN may regulate operations of agents of banks (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 72 of BOFIA concerns unclaimed funds in dormant accounts. It requires that after one year of inactivity, withdrawals require approval of:
opts: Two authorised signatories of the bank.
questionBank.exp: Section 72: After one year of no operation, withdrawal requires approval of two authorised signatories of the bank (p.18).

questionBank.q: Sections 74-78 of BOFIA establish the Banking Sector Resolution Fund. Which of the following contributes to the fund?
questionBank.exp: Sections 75-77: CBN contributes ₦10bn, NDIC ₦4bn, and each bank contributes 10 basis points of total assets (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 78 of BOFIA states that the Resolution Fund shall be utilised exclusively for purposes including:
opts: Paying operating costs of a bridge bank.
questionBank.exp: Section 78: Fund may be used to pay operating costs of a bridge bank, costs of transfer, credit facilities, etc. (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 97 of BOFIA permits the CBN to freeze a customer's account if the Governor has reason to believe transactions involve:
opts: A criminal offence under any law.
questionBank.exp: Section 97: CBN may freeze account if transactions involve criminal offence (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 99 of BOFIA empowers the Governor to:
opts: Reduce or increase monetary penalties for contraventions.
Establish the Special Tribunal for Recovery.
questionBank.exp: Section 99: Governor may reduce or increase monetary penalty payable for contravention (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 100 of BOFIA allows the Governor to exempt certain institutions from provisions of the Act by:
opts: A notice published in the media and Gazette.
A resolution of the National Assembly.
questionBank.exp: Section 100: Governor may exempt other financial institutions or non-interest banks by notice in print/electronic media and Gazette (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 101 of BOFIA empowers the CBN to:
questionBank.exp: Section 101: CBN may charge such fees as Board considers appropriate (p.19).

questionBank.q: Section 102 of BOFIA establishes the Special Tribunal for the Enforcement and Recovery of Eligible Loans. This tribunal:
opts: Has jurisdiction to recover eligible loans.
Has jurisdiction over all criminal matters.
Is composed solely of CBN staff.
questionBank.exp: Section 102: Establishes Special Tribunal to exercise jurisdiction conferred on it for recovery of eligible loans (p.19).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a legislation that impacts banking in Nigeria, besides BOFIA?
questionBank.exp: Other legislation includes CAMA 2020, NDIC Act, SEC Act, EFCC Act, Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act (p.19).

questionBank.q: The CBN's Prudential Guidelines were introduced in 1990 to standardise:
opts: Asset classification and loan loss provisioning.
questionBank.exp: The Guidelines were meant to guide asset classification and provisioning (p.19).

questionBank.q: The revised Prudential Guidelines of 2010 address all of the following EXCEPT:
questionBank.exp: The 2010 guidelines address risk management, corporate governance, KYC/AML, and loan loss provisioning, not interest rate determination (p.19).

questionBank.q: According to the Prudential Guidelines, a bank's credit policy must be approved by the Board of Directors and reviewed at least every:
questionBank.exp: Credit policy should be reviewed at least every three years (p.19).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, the total outstanding exposure by a bank to a single obligor or group of related borrowers shall not exceed:
questionBank.exp: Single obligor limit is 20% of shareholders' fund unimpaired by losses (p.20).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines define a 'large exposure' as any credit to a customer that is at least:
questionBank.exp: Large exposure is any credit that is at least 10% of shareholders' fund (p.20).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, exposure to all tiers of government and their agencies shall not exceed:
questionBank.exp: Exposure to government and agencies shall not exceed 10% of total credit portfolio (p.20).

questionBank.q: Regarding exposures to directors and related interests, the Prudential Guidelines define a significant shareholding as:
questionBank.exp: Significant shareholding is holding of at least 5% of a bank's equity (p.20).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, before granting a facility, banks must obtain a credit report from at least:
questionBank.exp: Banks must obtain credit report from at least two credit bureaux (p.20).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require banks to review their credit portfolio at least:
questionBank.exp: Credit portfolio should be reviewed at least once in a quarter (p.21).

questionBank.q: A credit facility is deemed non-performing when interest or principal is due and unpaid for:
questionBank.exp: Non-performing when due and unpaid for 90 days or more (p.21).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, a sub-standard facility is one on which principal or interest remains unpaid for more than 90 days but less than:
questionBank.exp: Sub-standard: outstanding for more than 90 days but less than 180 days (p.21).

questionBank.q: The provisioning rate for a sub-standard facility under the Prudential Guidelines is:
questionBank.exp: Sub-standard provision is 10% (p.21).

questionBank.q: A doubtful facility is one on which principal or interest remains outstanding for at least 180 days but less than 360 days. Its provisioning rate is:
questionBank.exp: Doubtful provision is 50% (p.21).

questionBank.q: A lost facility is one on which principal or interest remains outstanding for 360 days or more. Its provisioning rate is:
questionBank.exp: Lost provision is 100% (p.22).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines allow for 'haircut adjustments' on collateral for provisioning. For collateral to qualify, it must be:
opts: Perfected and realisable with no restrictions on sale.
Valued by the bank's internal staff.
questionBank.exp: Collateral must be perfected, realisable, and regularly valued with transparent method (p.22).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, revaluation of fixed assets is allowed only for:
opts: Land and buildings (own premises) and requires prior CBN approval.
questionBank.exp: Revaluation is applicable to own premises only and requires prior CBN approval (p.22).

questionBank.q: The revaluation surplus on fixed assets recognised in the books is discounted by:
questionBank.exp: The difference between market and historic value shall be discounted by 55% (p.22).

questionBank.q: The minimum capital adequacy ratio (CAR) prescribed by the CBN is:
questionBank.exp: Minimum CAR is 10% (p.22).

questionBank.q: A bank with a CAR between 5% and 10% is classified as:
questionBank.exp: Under capitalised: CAR greater than or equal to 5% but less than 10% (p.22-23).

questionBank.q: A bank with a CAR less than 5% but equal to or greater than 2% is classified as:
questionBank.exp: Significantly undercapitalised: CAR less than 5% but >=2% (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank with a CAR less than 2% is classified as:
questionBank.exp: Critically undercapitalised: CAR less than 2% (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank with a negative CAR is classified as:
questionBank.exp: Insolvent: negative CAR (p.23).

questionBank.q: For an undercapitalised bank (CAR 5-10%), which of the following is a supervisory action?
questionBank.exp: Under capitalised: special examination, restrict dividends, restrict investment in subsidiaries/fixed assets (p.23).

questionBank.q: For a significantly undercapitalised bank (CAR <5% but >=2%), CBN may:
questionBank.exp: Significantly undercapitalised: restrict new lending to recoveries, request business plan, etc. (p.23).

questionBank.q: For a critically undercapitalised bank (CAR <2%), CBN may:
opts: Take over management and control and/or revoke licence.
Require a business plan but not take over.
questionBank.exp: Critically undercapitalised: take over management and control and/or revoke licence (p.23).

questionBank.q: The CBN's circular on rendition of false returns (BSD/1/2003) is aimed at ensuring:
opts: Data integrity for proper administration and planning.
questionBank.exp: The circular ensures data integrity and punishes erring banks (p.23).

questionBank.q: CBN's foreign exchange management circulars forbid practices such as:
opts: Round tripping and non-disclosure of foreign accounts.
questionBank.exp: They forbid unlawful use of foreign exchange including round tripping, non-disclosure, etc. (p.23-24).

questionBank.q: The CBN prohibits borrowing from within the banking system to recapitalise banks. Funds borrowed outside the banking system must:
opts: Be of the type and nature that qualify as part of capital.
questionBank.exp: Outside funds must be of the type and nature that qualify as part of capital per CBN's Guidance Notes (p.24).

questionBank.q: The CBN's directive on currency substitution (April 2015) precludes:
opts: Pricing of goods and services in foreign currency within Nigeria.
Use of foreign currency for imports.
Payment of salaries in foreign currency.
questionBank.exp: The directive precludes charging in foreign currency for services in Nigeria (p.24).

questionBank.q: Under the CBN's whistleblowing policy, reports of dishonest conduct by CBN employees should be sent to:
opts: The Head, Ethics & Anti-Corruption Office, CBN.
questionBank.exp: Reports should be sent to Head, Ethics & Anti-Corruption Office, Governors' Department, CBN (p.24).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Regulation for management of foreign exchange risks limits a bank's aggregate foreign currency borrowing (excluding intergroup) to:
questionBank.exp: It should not exceed 75% of shareholders' funds unimpaired by losses (p.24).

questionBank.q: The CBN's measures on dud cheques include barring serial offenders from the clearing system for a period of:
questionBank.exp: Serial issuers are barred from clearing system for 5 years (p.24).

questionBank.q: The CBN's Know Your Customer (KYC) regulations require banks to:
opts: Identify and verify customer identity and monitor transactions.
Maintain customer deposits in foreign currency.
Provide loans only to verified customers.
questionBank.exp: KYC requires identification, verification, and monitoring to prevent money laundering (p.25).

questionBank.q: The Bank Verification Number (BVN) is a unique identifier assigned to each bank customer to:
opts: Track customer transactions for tax purposes.
questionBank.exp: BVN is used to verify identity and prevent fraud (p.25).

questionBank.q: The CBN's consumer protection initiatives include regulations on:
opts: Fees and charges, overdrafts, and debt collection.
questionBank.exp: Consumer protection covers fees, overdrafts, debt collection, etc. (p.25).

questionBank.q: The CBN's financial inclusion initiatives include:
opts: Mobile money and agent banking schemes.
questionBank.exp: Financial inclusion includes mobile money and agent banking (p.25).

questionBank.q: The CBN has adopted the Basel Accords to:
opts: Require banks to maintain certain levels of capital and liquidity.
questionBank.exp: Basel Accords require capital and liquidity to reduce systemic risk (p.25).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, a bank's credit policy should cover:
questionBank.exp: Credit policy should cover loan administration, disbursement, and appropriate monitoring (p.19).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require banks to have internal policies to control credit risk concentrations. Such policies must be approved by:
questionBank.exp: Credit concentration policies should be approved by the Board (p.20).

questionBank.q: According to the Prudential Guidelines, a bank must provide evidence of a search on the borrower in the CBN's Credit Risk Management System (CRMS) database:
questionBank.exp: Evidence of search in CRMS database should be provided before granting facility (p.20).

questionBank.q: A loan application form (LAF) must be completed before any exposure is approved. The LAF should contain:
opts: Recent audited financial statements and projected cash flows.
questionBank.exp: LAF should contain such information as financial statements, projected cash flows, etc. (p.20).

questionBank.q: A credit facility may be considered performing if:
opts: Payments of both principal and interest are up-to-date.
Principal is not paid but interest is up-to-date.
Principal is paid but interest is overdue for 30 days.
Principal and interest are overdue for 60 days.
questionBank.exp: Performing if payments of both principal and interest are up-to-date (p.21).

questionBank.q: A facility is non-performing if interest payments equal to 90 days of interest have been capitalised, rescheduled, or rolled over. This is known as:
questionBank.exp: Capitalised, rescheduled, or rolled over interest payments are considered non-performing (p.21).

questionBank.q: Subjective criteria for classifying a facility as sub-standard include:
opts: Inadequate cash flow to service debt.
questionBank.exp: Subjective criteria: inadequate cash flow, undercapitalisation, absence of financial information, irregular payments, etc. (p.21).

questionBank.q: A doubtful facility has a provisioning rate of 50%. This classification includes facilities on which principal or interest remains unpaid for at least 180 days but less than 360 days and:
opts: Are not secured by perfected realisable collateral.
questionBank.exp: Doubtful if not secured by legal title to leased assets or perfected realisable collateral (p.21).

questionBank.q: A lost facility is considered uncollectible and typically has a provision of 100%. Examples include:
opts: Facilities with overdue interest less than 90 days.
Facilities with collateral values covering exposure.
questionBank.exp: Lost facilities are those considered uncollectible, e.g., abandoned, secured with unmarketable securities, or extended to judgment debtors with no means (p.22).

questionBank.q: For collateral adjustments in loan provisioning (haircut), the collateral must be regularly valued with:
opts: Valuation by the bank's internal auditor.
questionBank.exp: Collateral must be regularly valued with transparent method of valuation (p.22).

questionBank.q: Revaluation of fixed assets can only be done after a minimum period of:
questionBank.exp: Revaluation permissible within a minimum period of seven years after purchase or last revaluation (p.22).

questionBank.q: The study guide mentions that the Federal Ministry of Finance formerly conducted on-site supervision of banks between 1960 and 1965. Which of the following is correct?
opts: CBN handled off-site, FMF handled on-site.
FMF handled off-site, CBN handled on-site.
Only the CBN handled all supervision.
questionBank.exp: Between 1960 and 1965, CBN handled off-site, FMF handled on-site (p.5).

questionBank.q: The harmonisation of regulations by the FSRCC is intended to address:
opts: Duplicity and conflicts among multiple regulators.
Increase in the number of banks.
questionBank.exp: FSRCC was created to harmonise due to duplicity and conflicts among regulators (p.7).

questionBank.q: The CBN's power to revoke a banking licence under Section 12 of BOFIA requires:
opts: The approval of the Board of CBN.
The approval of the Federal Ministry of Finance.
The approval of the National Assembly.
questionBank.exp: Section 12: Governor may, with approval of the Board, revoke licence (p.13).

questionBank.q: Section 19(6) of BOFIA defines 'director' for the purpose of related party transactions to include:
opts: The director's spouse, parents, siblings, and children, their spouses, and companies where the director holds at least 5%.
questionBank.exp: Section 19(6) expands director to include family members and companies in which director has at least 5% shareholding (p.15).

questionBank.q: Under BOFIA, a bank that fails to comply with obligations under the Act may have its licence revoked. This is provided in:
questionBank.exp: Section 12(g) includes failure to comply with obligations as grounds for revocation (p.14).

questionBank.q: The Banking Sector Resolution Fund established under BOFIA is domiciled with:
questionBank.exp: Section 74: Fund shall be domiciled with the CBN (p.18).

questionBank.q: The CBN's contribution to the Banking Sector Resolution Fund at commencement is ₦10 billion, as per:
questionBank.exp: Section 75: CBN contributes ₦10 billion (p.18).

questionBank.q: NDIC's contribution to the Banking Sector Resolution Fund at commencement is ₦4 billion, as per:
questionBank.exp: Section 76: NDIC contributes ₦4 billion (p.18).

questionBank.q: Each bank's contribution to the Banking Sector Resolution Fund is an amount equal to 10 basis points of total assets, as per:
questionBank.exp: Section 77: Each bank contributes 10 basis points of total assets (p.18).

questionBank.q: Section 94 of BOFIA empowers the CBN to:
opts: Manage and regulate operations of the Resolution Fund.
questionBank.exp: Section 94: CBN has power to manage and regulate operations of the Fund (p.18).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a ground for revocation of a bank's licence under Section 12 of BOFIA?
opts: Ceasing to carry on banking business for six continuous months.
questionBank.exp: Section 12 lists cessation, liquidation, failure to comply with conditions, insufficient assets, unsound conduct, threat to stability, non-compliance, critical undercapitalisation, failure to commence operations. Failure to pay dividends is not a ground (p.13-14).

questionBank.q: The CBN's circular on Reporting Unethical Conduct (BSD/DIR/GEN/LAB/08/017 of April 2, 2015) directs that reports be sent:
opts: Directly, confidentially, or anonymously to the Head, Ethics & Anti-Corruption Office.
questionBank.exp: The circular directs reports to Head, Ethics & Anti-Corruption Office (p.24).

questionBank.q: The CBN's measure to dissuade issuance of dud cheques includes forwarding names of offenders to:
questionBank.exp: Names are forwarded to Private Credit Bureaux and CRMS (p.24).

questionBank.q: If a bank fails to report a serial dud cheque issuer as required, the bank is considered to have:
opts: Concealed and misrepresented material fact and punished under BOFIA.
questionBank.exp: Failure to report is concealment and misrepresentation, punished under BOFIA (p.24-25).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a reason banks must adapt to regulatory changes?
opts: To comply with law and reduce risk.
questionBank.exp: Adaptation ensures compliance, reduces risk, improves efficiency, and maintains competitiveness (p.11).

questionBank.q: Market discipline as a regulatory principle means:
opts: Banks are required to disclose financial information to enable stakeholders to assess risk.
Banks are allowed to set their own capital requirements.
questionBank.exp: Market discipline requires disclosure to enable stakeholders to assess risk (p.12).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines were revised in 2010 to address the financial crisis of 2007/09. Which of the following was a key focus?
opts: Enhancing the quality of banks through improved risk management.
questionBank.exp: The revision aimed to enhance quality of banks, addressing risk management, corporate governance, KYC/AML, and loan provisioning (p.19).

questionBank.q: Under BOFIA, a bank that is designated as systemically important may be subject to:
questionBank.exp: Systemically important banks may be subject to additional oversight (p.17-18).

questionBank.q: Section 19(3)(c) of BOFIA prohibits a bank from remitting, in whole or in part, the debts owed to it by:
opts: Any of its directors or past directors.
questionBank.exp: Section 19(3)(c): Bank cannot remit debts owed by its directors or past directors (p.15).

questionBank.q: The Special Tribunal for the Enforcement and Recovery of Eligible Loans under Section 102 of BOFIA is composed and its membership is highlighted in:
questionBank.exp: Section 103 highlights membership and composition (p.19).

questionBank.q: The CBN's circular on foreign exchange management aims to ensure:
opts: Realisation of monetary policy objectives, check capital flight, and curb money laundering.
questionBank.exp: Essence is to ensure monetary policy objectives, check capital flight, and curb money laundering (p.23-24).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require that a bank's credit policy should be reviewed at least every:
questionBank.exp: Reviewed at least every three years (p.19).

questionBank.q: Under the Prudential Guidelines, the total outstanding exposure (on and off-balance sheet) by a bank to all tiers of government and their agencies shall not exceed 10% of:
questionBank.exp: Limitation is 10% of total credit portfolio (p.20).

questionBank.q: The Prudential Guidelines require banks to ensure that their credit policies specifically address lending to directors as part of:
opts: Related parties or insiders lending policies.
questionBank.exp: Credit policies should address lending to directors as related parties or insiders (p.20).

questionBank.q: A bank grants a loan of ₦50 million to a single company. The bank's shareholders' fund is ₦200 million. Is this within the single obligor limit?
opts: Yes, because it is 25% of shareholders' fund, exceeding the 20% limit.
No, because it is 25% which exceeds the 20% limit.
Yes, because it is 10% of shareholders' fund.
questionBank.exp: The limit is 20% of shareholders' fund (₦200m x 20% = ₦40m). ₦50m exceeds it, so it violates the limit (p.20).

questionBank.q: A bank classifies a loan as 'doubtful' when the principal has been unpaid for 200 days. What is the required provisioning rate?
questionBank.exp: Doubtful is 180-360 days and requires 50% provision (p.21).

questionBank.q: A bank's CAR falls to 4%. According to the Prudential Guidelines, this bank is classified as:
questionBank.exp: Significantly undercapitalised: CAR <5% but >=2% (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank's CAR is 1.5%. What supervisory action is most likely?
opts: Take over management and control and/or revoke licence.
questionBank.exp: Critically undercapitalised (CAR<2%) may lead to takeover and/or revocation (p.23).

questionBank.q: A bank that has negative CAR is considered insolvent, and the appropriate action is:
questionBank.exp: Insolvent banks (negative CAR) face licence revocation (p.23).

questionBank.q: Under Section 6 of BOFIA, which of the following requires prior CBN consent?
questionBank.exp: Section 6: No branch opening or closing without prior CBN consent (p.13).

questionBank.q: Section 7 of BOFIA requires CBN approval for:
opts: Any change in control or ownership structure of a bank.
Any change in the bank's auditors.
Any change in the bank's name.
questionBank.exp: Section 7: Restructuring, re-organisation, mergers, disposal, change of control require CBN approval (p.13).

questionBank.q: Under Section 12(b) of BOFIA, a bank's licence may be revoked if the bank:
questionBank.exp: Section 12(b): goes into liquidation or is wound up (p.13).

questionBank.q: Section 13 of BOFIA requires banks to maintain capital funds unimpaired by losses. The CBN may prescribe a CAR for each category. Failure to observe may lead to:
questionBank.exp: Penalties for failure may include fine, revocation, or other actions (p.14).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the NDIC under Section 2 of the NDIC Act?
opts: Insuring deposit liabilities of licensed banks.
Giving technical or financial assistance to insured institutions.
Approving mergers and acquisitions of banks.
questionBank.exp: Approving mergers is SEC's function, not NDIC's (p.5).

questionBank.q: Bank supervision is described as the process of monitoring banks to ensure their operations are:
opts: Safe and sound and in compliance with laws and regulations.
questionBank.exp: Supervision ensures safe and sound operations and compliance with laws (p.26).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a type of bank supervision?
questionBank.exp: Supervision is either on-site or off-site (p.25).

questionBank.q: On-site examination of a bank is carried out:
opts: At the premises of the regulator.
At the premises of the bank being reviewed.
questionBank.exp: On-site examination is carried out on the premises of the bank being reviewed (p.25).

questionBank.q: Off-site supervision involves:
opts: Receipt and analysis of mandatory statutory returns sent to the CBN.
questionBank.exp: Off-site supervision comprises receipt and analysis of statutory returns (p.26).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a reason why banks are supervised?
opts: Because they are guardians of people's wealth.
To increase the number of banks.
questionBank.exp: Banks are guardians of people's wealth and must be checked for the benefit of depositors and stakeholders (p.26).

questionBank.q: Bank examination looks at all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: How much risk the bank undertakes.
What resources are available to support business and risk profile.
questionBank.exp: Examination looks at risk, management, and resources, not marketing strategies (p.26).

questionBank.q: The impact of bank supervision on the financial system includes:
questionBank.exp: Supervision contributes to stability, transparency, deposit protection, and compliance (p.26-27).

questionBank.q: Routine on-site examination of banks is presently conducted how often?
questionBank.exp: Routine on-site examination is conducted twice a year (p.27).

questionBank.q: The two types of routine on-site examinations mentioned are:
opts: Risk Assets assessment and Risk Based Supervision.
questionBank.exp: Routine examinations are Risk Assets assessment and Risk Based Supervision (p.27).

questionBank.q: Nigeria has adopted which approach to banking supervision in line with international best practice?
questionBank.exp: Nigeria has opted for a Risk-based Supervision (RBS) approach (p.27).

questionBank.q: Risk Based Supervision (RBS) involves:
opts: Identifying significant activities and determining inherent risks.
Only checking compliance with capital ratios.
questionBank.exp: RBS involves identification of activities, determination of risks, evaluation of risk management, and determination of overall riskiness (p.27).

questionBank.q: Macro-prudential supervision aims to:
opts: Complement micro-prudential supervision by considering threats to the whole financial system.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential supervision complements traditional supervision of individual banks with consideration of systemic threats (p.27).

questionBank.q: The ultimate goal of macro-prudential supervision is to:
opts: Minimise systemic risk that could damage the broader economy.
questionBank.exp: Goal is to minimise systemic risk that could inflict significant damage on the broader economy (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which type of examination is conducted as at the financial year end of every bank (31st December)?
questionBank.exp: Routine Risk Assessment Examination is conducted as at the financial year end (p.28).

questionBank.q: The Routine Risk Assessment Examination primarily reviews:
opts: All assets on the balance sheet to check for impairments.
questionBank.exp: It reviews all assets on the balance sheet for impairments (p.28).

questionBank.q: A special examination is conducted when:
opts: The regulatory authorities have cause to believe safety and soundness have been impaired.
The bank opens a new branch.
questionBank.exp: Special examination is conducted when safety and soundness are considerably impaired (p.28).

questionBank.q: A special examination is a statutory examination and is:
opts: Conducted only at the bank's request.
questionBank.exp: It is a prelude to regulatory intervention (p.28).

questionBank.q: Foreign Exchange Examination is conducted to check compliance with:
questionBank.exp: It checks compliance with forex rules and regulations (p.28).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are unscheduled examinations arising from:
opts: Petitions from the banking public or suspicions.
questionBank.exp: Special investigations arise from petitions, suspicions, or prior examination activities (p.28).

questionBank.q: At the end of every examination, a report of findings is produced. The report must be:
opts: Factual and supported by credible documentary evidence.
questionBank.exp: Reports must be factual and assertions supported with evidence (p.28-29).

questionBank.q: Examination findings must be discussed with management, and management explanations must be factored into the final report. This is described as:
questionBank.exp: It is an open reporting system with no surprises (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of bank examination?
questionBank.exp: Types: Routine Risk Assessment, Special, Foreign Exchange, and Special Investigations. Financial Audit is not listed (p.28).

questionBank.q: The CBN and NDIC carry out examinations to determine:
opts: Solvency status and compliance with laws.
questionBank.exp: Examinations determine solvency and compliance (p.25).

questionBank.q: Early Warning Signals (EWS) are used to:
opts: Detect ill-health and take prompt corrective action.
questionBank.exp: EWS detects ill-health and leads to Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) (p.26).

questionBank.q: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) refers to:
opts: Taking appropriate action to restore a troubled bank to good standing.
Immediate liquidation of any troubled bank.
questionBank.exp: PCA is taking appropriate corrective action to restore a troubled bank (p.26).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an objective of bank supervision?
opts: To ensure compliance with regulations and laws.
questionBank.exp: Supervision ensures compliance and protection (p.26-27).

questionBank.q: Bank supervision helps to promote:
questionBank.exp: Supervision promotes operational resilience, among other benefits (p.27).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a component of the supervisory structure?
questionBank.exp: Supervisory structure includes licensing, capital, accounting, disclosure, risk management (p.10).

questionBank.q: The Basel Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision include the principle that supervisors should have:
opts: Power to revoke licences and take corrective actions.
questionBank.exp: Core Principles include supervisory powers like revocation and corrective actions (p.10).

questionBank.q: Nigeria's compliance with the 29 Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision is described as:
questionBank.exp: Nigeria is largely compliant with the Core Principles (p.27).

questionBank.q: Risk-based supervision focuses on:
opts: The overall riskiness of the bank's business.
questionBank.exp: RBS determines the overall riskiness of the bank's business (p.27).

questionBank.q: The macro-prudential approach is concerned with:
opts: The stability of the financial system as a whole.
questionBank.exp: Macro-prudential approach focuses on systemic stability (p.27).

questionBank.q: Special investigations are typically triggered by:
questionBank.exp: They arise from petitions, suspicions, or prior examinations (p.28).

questionBank.q: The report of examination findings is described as an open reporting system because:
opts: Findings are discussed with management and their responses included.
Findings are shared with all banks.
Findings are available to the public.
questionBank.exp: It is open because findings are discussed with management and responses factored in (p.29).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a benefit of off-site supervision?
opts: It is less costly than on-site.
It allows physical verification of assets.
It provides real-time insight into bank operations.
It reduces the need for statutory returns.
questionBank.exp: Off-site is less costly, though it relies on returns (p.26).

questionBank.q: Regulatory authorities in emerging markets often rely more on off-site supervision because:
questionBank.exp: Emerging markets with inadequate resources rely more on off-site supervision (p.26).

questionBank.q: Bank supervision is critical to mitigate:
questionBank.exp: Banking crisis is best mitigated through effective supervision (p.26).

questionBank.q: The Asset Management Corporation of Nigeria (AMCON) was established to:
opts: Purchase toxic risk assets of ailing banks.
